passage: "Screenshot, please," said Dhruv, his friend, at the gate, holding out a phone. Yogesh sighed and showed his screen: four hours twenty. "Ouch." "Yours?" Dhruv turned his own. "Three fifty. Yesterday was five. You are not beating me." "Bet I will tomorrow." "Loser buys the samosas on Friday." They shook on it. That night at ten Yogesh's phone buzzed: a screenshot showing 3:10. He sent back 2:55. At the gate next morning Dhruv groaned. "You are on fire. Did you actually put it down?" "In the drawer." "Fine. Rematch tonight, and I am walking to the library first so I cannot cheat with a scroll."

qa.q: What did the loser have to buy on Friday?
qa.a: The loser had to buy the samosas.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about beating Dhruv?
qa.a: Pleased and competitive, since he sent back a lower number after saying he would win.

qa.q: What could the friends do if the contest starts to feel stressful?
qa.a: Make the goal shared, such as both staying under a number, because cooperation keeps it friendly.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see the challenge?
qa.a: As a friendly rivalry, since Dhruv groaned but asked for a rematch.

grounding: Two friends compare a daily screen-time screenshot each night, and the small social stakes turn the limit into a friendly challenge.

subtype: Approach: accountability partner for screen limits [Action]
passage: I'm Devika, and last term Tejas and I made a deal that sounded too small to work. Every night at ten, we'd each send the other a screenshot of our screen time for the day. No lectures, no punishments, just the number. The first night mine said five hours ten. I almost didn't send it. Tejas sent back four hours forty and a sweating emoji. After that, the number mattered more than it should have. I'd be halfway into a video and think, Tejas will see this. By the second week it had turned into a game: whoever was lower got to pick a song the other had to listen to. I got down to two hours most days. Tejas still wins more often, which is annoying.

qa.q: What time did they send the screenshots?
Why did Devika almost not send the first screenshot?
qa.a: Devika felt embarrassed about five hours ten and didn't want Tejas to see it.

qa.q: What could keep the deal working once the novelty wears off?
qa.a: Setting a shared target and changing the small prize now and then, so the friendly challenge stays fun.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about the deal?
qa.a: Tejas seems to enjoy it, joking with a sweating emoji and winning more often, so the challenge helps both friends.

grounding: A student recalls swapping nightly screen-time screenshots with a friend, where small social stakes turned limits into a friendly challenge.

subtype: Approach: accountability partner for screen limits [Action]
passage:
Warden's log, boys' hostel, 18 September
Ramesh and Sohail from Room 12 were on my list last month: both on phones past midnight most nights. I spoke to them once, and it made no difference. This week I noticed a change, so I asked. They showed me their arrangement: at 10 pm, each sends the other a screenshot of that day's screen time. Whoever has the higher number makes tea for both at breakfast. Ramesh said for the first few days he "couldn't bear" letting Sohail see his total, so he started stopping earlier. Now they compare numbers at breakfast like cricket scores. Lights have been off by 11 in Room 12 four nights running. I have not said anything. It is working better than my talk did.
— Irfan

qa.q: What does the loser of the screenshot deal have to do?
qa.a: Make tea for both at breakfast.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel about Sohail seeing his total at first?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, saying he couldn't bear letting Sohail see it, which pushed him to stop earlier.

qa.q: Why does the deal work better than the warden's talk?
qa.a: The small stakes come from a friend and a fun forfeit, so the limit feels real and even enjoyable rather than imposed.

qa.q: How does Irfan see the change in Room 12?
qa.a: Irfan notices lights off by 11 and chooses not to interfere, admitting the boys' own arrangement works better than the earlier talk.

grounding: A warden's log shows two friends exchanging nightly screen-time screenshots, with small stakes turning the limit into a friendly contest.
